tagline: Scores a draft live against the pages already ranking, term by term.
verdictSummary: The mechanic is honest arithmetic: take the pages currently ranking, extract their meaningful terms, and compare your draft's usage against the distribution. Everything about that is reproducible except the input, because getting the ranking pages means a SERP API with a bill attached. What is genuinely worth building is the transparency — a score you can see the formula for, in an editor that updates as you type, rather than a number that goes up for reasons nobody explains.
coreLoopDIY: Fetch the pages currently ranking for your target query, extract their term distribution, and write in an editor that scores your draft against it live and tells you exactly which terms are under- or over-used.
whatYouLose: the SERP data, which stays a paid API call per query
the scoring model tuned against thousands of real ranking outcomes
the AI drafting and rewriting built into the same editor
the integrations that push a finished draft into a CMS
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the score is only meaningful if it correlates with ranking, and that correlation is the part a vendor has tuned against far more outcomes than you will ever observe.
notes: Live in-editor scoring with a visible formula is the angle, deliberately distinct from the brief-generation and element-comparison approaches taken by the other content-optimisation entries in this catalogue.
prompt:
Build a content editor that scores a draft against the pages currently ranking for a target query, with the formula fully visible.

Corpus collection: for a target query, fetch the top 10 organic results through a commercial SERP API behind a swappable provider module, never by scraping. Then fetch each result page politely, honouring robots.txt, and extract its main content — strip navigation, footer, cookie banners and sidebars with a boilerplate-removal pass, because scoring against a competitor's navigation menu produces nonsense. Store the corpus with its collection date; a corpus older than a few weeks is stale and the interface should say so.

Term extraction: from the corpus, extract unigrams, bigrams and trigrams, drop stopwords, lemmatise, and compute for each term: the number of corpus pages containing it (document frequency), and the median count per page among the pages that use it. Rank terms by document frequency first — a term nine of ten pages use is a stronger signal than one that appears thirty times on a single page.

The editor: a plain writing surface with the term panel beside it, updating as the user types, debounced. For every term in the target list, show the median usage across the corpus, the draft's current count, and a state: missing, under, in range, over. Group terms into essential (in eight or more corpus pages), recommended (five to seven), and optional. Clicking a term highlights every occurrence in the draft.

The score: a single 0-100 number, and immediately beneath it, the arithmetic — how many essential terms are covered, how many recommended, how far the draft's length sits from the corpus median, and the weight of each component. Let the user adjust the weights. A score whose derivation is hidden is a score nobody can argue with, and arguing with it is exactly what a writer should be doing.

Guard against the obvious failure: flag any term used more than twice the corpus median as over-used, and show a warning that writing to satisfy a term list produces text nobody wants to read. The tool measures coverage; it does not certify quality.

Headings: extract the corpus's H2 and H3 texts, cluster them, and present the common subtopics as an outline suggestion, with the source pages listed for each.

Export: the draft as Markdown, and the term list plus scores as CSV.

Out of scope: generating or rewriting text with a model, rank tracking, backlink data, and CMS publishing.

faq.q: Can I import my NeuronWriter projects?
faq.a: Term lists and drafts export as text and can be pasted in, but the scores will not match because this build computes its own from its own corpus. In practice you re-run the analysis on the same query, which costs one SERP call.

faq.q: Does hitting the score actually improve rankings?
faq.a: Nobody outside a search engine can answer that honestly, including the paid tools. What term coverage reliably does is stop you omitting subtopics your competitors all cover, which is a real and modest benefit. Treat the number as a checklist, not a target, which is why the prompt shows its own arithmetic and warns about over-use.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: One SERP API call per target query, so one to three tenths of a cent, plus free page fetches. Analysing fifty articles costs well under a dollar against a monthly subscription — this is one of the clearest cost wins in the SEO category.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Calibration. Your score is arithmetic over ten pages; theirs is arithmetic tuned against how thousands of pages actually performed. The shape of the advice is the same and the confidence behind it is not.
